newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open weaker, eye on supply.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open weaker, eye on supply.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices opened lower on Tuesday, hours ahead of the bidding deadline for the first leg of the Treasury's three-part quarterly refunding operation.
The Treasury will sell $16.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday. The bidding deadline for the notes is 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
The three-year note auction is due to be followed by sales of $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.
In early trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 6/32 to 101-23/32, yielding 6.49 percent.
"Supply is coming," said James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch. "That's the main thing today."
Blumenthal said the three-year auction ought to go well if the market does not start to rally.
With the when-issued yield at six percent, there should be sufficient demand for the issue, he said.
"With the economic data coming out being minor, the market will focus on the auction and upcoming supply of 10- and 30-year notes," he said.
"You get the (Conference Board's) leading indicators, but that's minor and really everyone knows what it is so it's not something that's going to move the markets," said Blumenthal.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that the leading economic indicators index rose 0.1 percent in June after rising 0.3 percent in May.
The market also gets two weekly reports on chain and department store sales on Tuesday.
The seasonally adjusted BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index is due at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT, although the result is typically rumored in the market before then.
The index rose 0.4 percent in the week ended July 26 from the prior week. No forecast was available for the week ended August 2.

The Redbook chain and department store sales measure is due by 1400 EDT/1800 GMT. For the week ended July 26, it rose 0.1 percent. No forecast was available for that measure, either, for the week ended August 2.
The Commerce Department's release on June housing completions (at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT) is "another minor number" that should have no market impact, said Blumenthal.
Analysts said the market's retreat from the peaks it reached last week would help the auctions attract demand.
The benchmark 30-year bond yield fell as low as 6.29 percent last week before backing up to 6.50 percent by Tuesday morning.
The higher yields and cheaper prices should make the new notes and bonds more attractive to buyers, analysts said.
"If the market can keep the when-issued yield for the three-year note at six percent, that would be a help," said Blumenthal.
Trading on a when-issued basis, the three-year notes to be sold Tuesday were yielding 6.035 percent in early dealings.
The ten-year notes to be sold on Wednesday yielded 6.225 percent on a when-issued basis. The 30-year bonds to be sold on Thursday were yielding 6.475 percent.
In early dealings, the two-year Treasury note unchanged at 99-30/32 to yield 5.91 percent.
The five-year note was down 2/32 to 99-15/32 to yield 6.13 percent.
Ten-year notes were down 2/32 at 102-27/32 to yield 6.23 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.14 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.20 percent and 5.23 percent, respectively.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
